title: System of Particles and Rotational Motion

topics.title: Rigid bodies and the kinds of motion

learn.hook: A rolling cricket ball, a spinning ceiling fan and a car on a highway: one translates, one rotates, one does both. Rigid-body physics handles all three.
points: An extended body is a system of particles. A rigid body is an idealisation in which the distances between all pairs of particles stay fixed.
Pure translation: every particle has the same velocity at every instant (a block sliding down an incline).
Rotation about a fixed axis: every particle moves in a circle in a plane perpendicular to the axis, with its centre on the axis (ceiling fan, potter's wheel).
Rotation about a fixed point (not a fixed axis): e.g. a spinning top whose axis itself swings around a vertical line (precession).
General motion of a rigid body = translation (of a reference point, like the centre of mass) + rotation about an axis through it (a rolling wheel).

example.q: A cylinder rolls down an incline without slipping. Is its motion pure translation?
steps: Points at the top, centre and bottom of the cylinder have different velocities at the same instant.
So it cannot be pure translation.
It is translation of the centre plus rotation about the axis through the centre.

topics.title: Centre of mass of particles and laminas

learn.hook: A gymnast's centre of mass can even lie outside her body during a back-bend. It is a point defined by maths, not by matter.
points: Two particles on a line: X = (m₁x₁ + m₂x₂)/(m₁ + m₂). For equal masses it is midway.
n particles in 3D: R = Σmᵢrᵢ/M, i.e. X = Σmᵢxᵢ/M, Y = Σmᵢyᵢ/M, Z = Σmᵢzᵢ/M.
Continuous bodies: X = (1/M)∫x dm etc. For a uniform symmetric body (rod, ring, disc, sphere, cube) the CM lies at the geometric centre.
Uniform triangular lamina: CM at the centroid (intersection of medians).
Composite shapes (e.g. an L-shaped lamina of three equal squares): treat each part as a point mass at its own centre, then combine.

topics.title: Motion of the centre of mass

learn.hook: A Diwali rocket bursts into sparks high in the sky. The sparks fly everywhere, but their centre of mass calmly continues on the same parabola.
points: Differentiating MR = Σmᵢrᵢ: MV = Σmᵢvᵢ and MA = Σmᵢaᵢ.
MA = F_ext: the CM moves like a single particle of mass M acted on by the total external force.
Internal forces between particles cancel in third-law pairs, so they cannot affect the motion of the CM.
Exploding projectile: the explosion forces are internal, so the CM keeps following the original parabola (until fragments hit the ground).
The translational motion of a system is the motion of its CM; the rest is motion relative to the CM.

example.q: A shell fired as a projectile explodes into two equal parts at the top of its path. One part falls straight down. Where does the CM land, and where does the other part land?
steps: The CM continues on the original parabola, so it lands at the original range R.
One half lands at R/2 (below the top).
Since the CM is midway between equal halves, the other half lands at 3R/2.
example.answer: CM at R; other piece at 3R/2

topics.title: Linear momentum of a system and its conservation

learn.hook: Two stars orbit each other in a binary system. They whirl around wildly, yet their centre of mass glides through space in a straight line.
points: Total momentum P = Σmᵢvᵢ = MV.
dP/dt = F_ext: only external forces change the total momentum.
If F_ext = 0, P is constant, so the CM moves with constant velocity (or stays at rest).
Radioactive decay of a nucleus at rest: the products fly apart in opposite directions so that the CM stays at rest.
Binary stars: under their mutual gravity (internal), the CM moves uniformly while the stars orbit around it.

example.q: A uranium-238 nucleus at rest decays into a thorium nucleus (234 u) and an alpha particle (4 u) moving at 1.17 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹. Find the thorium speed.
steps: Initial P = 0, so the products' momenta are equal and opposite.
v = 2 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹, opposite to the alpha particle.

learn.hook: Tighten a screw clockwise and it goes in. That everyday rule is exactly how the direction of a cross product is decided.
points: a × b = ab sin θ n̂, where n̂ is perpendicular to both a and b. Direction by the right-hand rule (fingers from a to b, thumb gives a × b) or a right-handed screw.
Properties: anticommutative (a × b = −b × a), distributive, and a × a = 0.
Unit vectors: î × ĵ = k̂, ĵ × k̂ = î, k̂ × î = ĵ; reversing the order gives a minus sign; î × î = 0.
Component (determinant) form: a × b = (a_yb_z − a_zb_y)î + (a_zbₓ − aₓb_z)ĵ + (aₓb_y − a_ybₓ)k̂.
Under reflection, ordinary (polar) vectors change sign but a × b does not: the cross product is an axial (pseudo) vector.

learn.hook: Planets sweep around the Sun for billions of years without slowing down because there is no external torque on them about the Sun.

learn.hook: Turning a car's steering wheel with both hands applies a couple: it spins the wheel without pushing it anywhere.
points: Mechanical equilibrium of a rigid body: net external force = 0 (translational) AND net external torque = 0 (rotational).

learn.hook: Tall structures, from the Qutub Minar to modern Mumbai skyscrapers, stand safely because their centre of gravity lies low and well within a wide base.
points: Centre of gravity (CG): the point where the total gravitational torque on the body is zero. In a uniform g, the CG coincides with the CM.

topics.title: Moment of inertia and radius of gyration

learn.hook: A tightrope walker carries a long pole. Spreading mass far from the axis makes her much harder to topple: that's moment of inertia.
points: Rotational KE: K = ½Iω², with moment of inertia I = Σmᵢrᵢ² (rᵢ = distance from the axis). Unit kg m².
I depends on the mass, its distribution, and the axis chosen. It is the rotational analogue of mass (measure of rotational inertia).
Thin ring about its axis (through centre, ⊥ plane): MR². Thin rod about a ⊥ axis through its centre: ML²/12.
Standard values: disc or solid cylinder about its axis MR²/2; hollow cylinder about its axis MR²; ring about a diameter MR²/2; disc about a diameter MR²/4; solid sphere about a diameter (2/5)MR².

topics.title: Angular momentum about a fixed axis and its conservation

learn.hook: A Bharatanatyam dancer spinning on one foot pulls her arms in and suddenly whirls faster. No push, just angular momentum conservation.
points: For rotation about a fixed axis: L = Iω, and dL/dt = τ (axial component).
If the external torque is zero, Iω = constant: I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂.
Examples: a person on a rotating stool pulling in arms (I decreases, ω increases); a diver tucking in to somersault faster; a skater spinning.
Rotational KE changes: K = L²/(2I). With L fixed, reducing I increases K; the extra energy comes from the work done by the person's muscles.
Typical numericals: torque on a disc from τ = Iα, L = Iω, and K = ½Iω².
